questions.q: Which type of muscle is striated but involuntary?
questions.explain: Cardiac muscle shows cross-striations like skeletal muscle, but it is not under voluntary control. It is regulated by its own pacemaker and modulated by the autonomic nervous system.

open.q: Which type of muscle is striated but involuntary?

questions.q: Which muscle type is both non-striated and involuntary?
questions.explain: Smooth muscle has no sarcomere pattern, so it looks non-striated. It is controlled by autonomic nerves, hormones and local factors.

open.q: Which muscle type is both non-striated and involuntary?

questions.q: Which statement about the nuclei of the three muscle types is correct?
options: Skeletal: many and peripheral; cardiac: usually one, central; smooth: one, central
Skeletal: one, central; cardiac: many, peripheral; smooth: many, central
All three have a single central nucleus
Skeletal: many, central; cardiac: none; smooth: many, peripheral
questions.explain: Skeletal fibres form by fusion of myoblasts, so they are multinucleated with nuclei pushed to the periphery under the sarcolemma. Cardiac and smooth muscle cells usually have one central nucleus.

questions.q: Intercalated discs are a feature of:
questions.explain: Intercalated discs join cardiac cells end to end. They contain gap junctions, which let the heart act as a functional syncytium, and desmosomes, which hold the cells together.

open.q: Intercalated discs are a feature of which muscle type?

questions.q: Skeletal muscle is normally controlled by:
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle contracts only when its somatic motor neuron fires, so it is voluntary and fully dependent on its nerve supply.

open.q: What normally controls skeletal muscle?

questions.q: Which muscle type depends entirely on its motor nerve to start a contraction?
questions.explain: Cardiac muscle is myogenic and has its own pacemaker. Smooth muscle can respond to stretch, hormones and local chemicals without a nerve signal. Skeletal muscle cannot contract without nerve stimulation.

open.q: Which muscle type depends entirely on its motor nerve to start a contraction?

questions.q: Which regulatory protein of skeletal muscle is absent from smooth muscle?
questions.explain: Smooth muscle has no troponin. Calcium binds calmodulin instead, which activates myosin light-chain kinase and phosphorylates the myosin light chain. Smooth muscle does contain tropomyosin.

open.q: Which regulatory protein of skeletal muscle is absent from smooth muscle?

questions.q: Type I (red, slow oxidative) skeletal muscle fibres are characterised by:
options: Many mitochondria, high myoglobin, slow contraction and resistance to fatigue
Few mitochondria, low myoglobin, fast contraction and rapid fatigue
Large glycogen stores and mainly anaerobic metabolism
The largest diameter and the highest myosin ATPase activity
questions.explain: Red fibres rely on oxidative metabolism, so they have many mitochondria, rich blood supply and myoglobin (which gives the red colour). They contract slowly and fatigue late.

open.q: What characterises Type I (red, slow oxidative) skeletal muscle fibres?

questions.q: Compared with red fibres, white (fast glycolytic) fibres have:
options: Larger diameter, more glycogen and glycolytic enzymes, and earlier fatigue
questions.explain: White fibres produce ATP mainly by anaerobic glycolysis. They give fast, powerful contractions but fatigue quickly.

open.q: How do white (fast glycolytic) fibres compare with red fibres?

questions.q: Muscles that hold posture for long periods, such as the soleus, contain mainly:
questions.explain: Postural muscles need contractions that can be sustained for hours without fatiguing, which suits oxidative slow fibres.

open.q: Which fibre type predominates in muscles that hold posture, such as the soleus?

questions.q: Which is an example of single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle?
options: Wall of the uterus or intestine
questions.explain: Single-unit smooth muscle has many gap junctions, so the fibres contract together as one unit. It often shows spontaneous (myogenic) activity. The other options are multiunit.

open.q: Give an example of single-unit (visceral) smooth muscle.

questions.q: Multiunit smooth muscle differs from single-unit smooth muscle in that it:
options: Has few gap junctions, and each fibre is separately innervated
Forms the wall of the gut
questions.explain: Each multiunit fibre acts almost independently, which allows fine, graded control, as in the ciliary muscle, the iris and arrector pili.

open.q: How does multiunit smooth muscle differ from single-unit smooth muscle?

questions.q: The structural and functional contractile unit of skeletal muscle is the:
questions.explain: A myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres joined end to end. Each sarcomere shortens when its filaments slide.

open.q: What is the structural and functional contractile unit of skeletal muscle?

questions.q: A sarcomere extends from:
options: One Z line to the next Z line
One M line to the next M line
One A band to the next I band
The H zone to the M line
questions.explain: Z lines mark the boundaries of the sarcomere. Its length at rest is roughly 2 µm.

open.q: Between which structures does a sarcomere extend?
accept: one z line to the next

questions.q: Which band contains only thin (actin) filaments and shortens during contraction?
questions.explain: Each I band spans two neighbouring sarcomeres, with a Z line in its middle. It is the light band, and it gets narrower as thin filaments slide into the A band.

open.q: Which band contains only thin (actin) filaments and shortens during contraction?

questions.q: The A band represents:
options: The full length of the thick (myosin) filaments, including their overlap with thin filaments
Only the region without any filament overlap
questions.explain: The A band is the dark band and its width equals the length of the thick filaments, which does not change during contraction.

open.q: What does the A band represent?

questions.q: The H zone is:
options: The central region of the A band containing only thick filaments in a relaxed sarcomere
The region of the I band without filaments
The line that joins thin filaments
questions.explain: The H zone has no thin-filament overlap in a relaxed muscle. The M line runs through its middle and holds the thick filaments in register.

open.q: What is the H zone?
accept: central region of A band with only thick filaments
region of A band without overlap

questions.q: Which structure anchors the thin filaments at the ends of the sarcomere?
questions.explain: Actin filaments attach to the Z line, mainly through alpha-actinin. The M line is the central anchor for thick filaments.

open.q: Which structure anchors the thin filaments at the ends of the sarcomere?

questions.q: The thick filament is made of:
questions.explain: A thick filament is a bundle of many myosin molecules, each with two heads projecting outward.

open.q: What is the thick filament made of?

questions.q: The globular head of the myosin molecule has:
options: ATPase activity and an actin-binding site
The attachment to the M line
questions.explain: The heads (part of heavy meromyosin) bind actin and hydrolyse ATP. They form the cross-bridges. The tail (light meromyosin) forms the thick filament backbone.

open.q: What two features does the globular head of the myosin molecule have?
accept: atpase activity and actin binding site

questions.q: The thin filament is made of:
questions.explain: F-actin forms the core, tropomyosin lies along its grooves, and troponin sits at intervals along the tropomyosin.

open.q: What is the thin filament made of?

questions.q: Which troponin subunit binds calcium?
questions.explain: Troponin C binds Ca²⁺, troponin I inhibits the actin–myosin interaction, and troponin T attaches the complex to tropomyosin.

open.q: Which troponin subunit binds calcium?

questions.q: The main role of titin is to:
options: Anchor thick filaments to the Z line, keep them centred and provide passive elasticity
Store calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Cover the active sites on actin
questions.explain: Titin is the largest known protein. It acts like a spring that returns a stretched sarcomere to its resting length.

open.q: What is the main role of titin?
accept: anchors thick filaments to z line

questions.q: A triad in skeletal muscle consists of:
options: One T tubule flanked by two terminal cisterns of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Two T tubules and one terminal cistern
One Z line and two M lines
questions.explain: In mammalian skeletal muscle, triads lie at the junction of the A and I bands. The T tubule membrane is next to the terminal cisterns, where calcium is released.

open.q: What does a triad in skeletal muscle consist of?
accept: one t tubule and two terminal cisterns
t tubule with two terminal cisternae
t tubule and two sr cisterns

questions.q: Why are T tubules important?
options: They carry the action potential from the sarcolemma deep into the fibre so that all sarcomeres contract together
questions.explain: Without T tubules, the centre of a thick fibre would contract late, because the signal would have to diffuse in from the surface.

open.q: Why are T tubules important?
accept: carry action potential into the fibre
carry action potential deep into fibre

questions.q: Calcium for skeletal muscle contraction is mainly stored in:
options: Terminal cisterns of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explain: The SR stores Ca²⁺ at high concentration, partly bound to calsequestrin, and releases it when the fibre is stimulated.

open.q: Where is calcium for skeletal muscle contraction mainly stored?

questions.q: From outermost to innermost, the connective tissue coverings of skeletal muscle are:
questions.explain: The epimysium surrounds the whole muscle, the perimysium surrounds each fascicle, and the endomysium surrounds each individual fibre.

open.q: Name the connective tissue coverings of skeletal muscle, from outermost to innermost.

questions.q: Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from absence of dystrophin, which normally:
options: Links the actin cytoskeleton to the sarcolemma
Binds calcium in the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Anchors myosin to the Z line
questions.explain: Without dystrophin, the sarcolemma tears during contraction and fibres degenerate. The gene is on the X chromosome, so the disease is X-linked recessive.

open.q: Duchenne muscular dystrophy results from absence of dystrophin. What does dystrophin normally do?
accept: connects actin cytoskeleton to cell membrane

questions.q: In the region of overlap, the ratio of thin to thick filaments in cross-section is:
questions.explain: Each thick filament is surrounded by six thin filaments, and each thin filament is shared by three thick filaments, which gives 2 thin per 1 thick.

open.q: In the region of overlap, what is the ratio of thin to thick filaments in cross-section?

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a basic property of skeletal muscle?
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle needs nerve stimulation and has no pacemaker. Its basic properties are excitability, contractility, extensibility and elasticity.

questions.q: Elasticity of muscle is the ability to:
options: Return to its original length after being stretched
Be stretched beyond its original length
questions.explain: Extensibility is the ability to be stretched, and elasticity is the ability to recoil after the stretch.

open.q: What is elasticity of muscle?
accept: returns to original length after stretch

questions.q: Which sequence describes a single muscle twitch?
options: Latent period → contraction period → relaxation period
questions.explain: In a typical twitch record, relaxation takes longer than contraction.

open.q: Name the three phases of a single muscle twitch, in order.
accept: latent period, contraction period, relaxation period

questions.q: The latent period of a muscle twitch is:
options: The interval between the stimulus and the start of visible shortening
questions.explain: No shortening is visible during this time, but the action potential, excitation–contraction coupling and cross-bridge formation are under way.

open.q: What is the latent period of a muscle twitch?
accept: interval between stimulus and start of shortening

questions.q: Cooling a skeletal muscle (within physiological limits) will:
options: Prolong the twitch, with slower contraction and relaxation
Have no effect on twitch duration
questions.explain: Enzyme-driven steps such as ATP hydrolysis and calcium reuptake slow down in the cold. Moderate warming has the opposite effect and speeds up the twitch.

open.q: What effect does cooling a skeletal muscle (within physiological limits) have on the twitch?

questions.q: As the load on a contracting muscle increases, the velocity of shortening:
questions.explain: Velocity is highest with no load. When the load equals the maximum force the muscle can generate, velocity falls to zero and the contraction is isometric.

open.q: As the load on a contracting muscle increases, what happens to the velocity of shortening?

questions.q: The staircase phenomenon (treppe) is:
options: A progressive increase in the force of the first few contractions in a rested muscle stimulated repeatedly
A progressive decrease in force due to fatigue
A sustained contraction at high stimulation frequency
questions.explain: Calcium accumulates in the sarcoplasm because the SR pump cannot remove it fully between rapid stimuli, so each contraction is slightly stronger. It is the physiological basis of a warm-up.

open.q: What is the staircase phenomenon (treppe)?
accept: progressive increase in force of first few contractions
increasing force with repeated stimulation of rested muscle

questions.q: Complete tetanus occurs when:
options: Stimulus frequency is high enough that successive twitches fuse with no relaxation between them
A single stimulus is very strong
questions.explain: Summation of twitches produces tetanus. At lower frequencies, partial relaxation occurs between twitches (incomplete tetanus). Normal voluntary contraction involves tetanic fusion.

open.q: When does complete tetanus occur?

questions.q: Why can a whole skeletal muscle give graded contractions when a single fibre obeys the all-or-none law?
options: The number of fibres (motor units) recruited varies with the strength of the signal
Sarcomere length changes with stimulus strength
The all-or-none law does not apply to muscle
questions.explain: Each fibre either contracts or does not. A stronger command recruits more motor units, and a higher firing frequency adds temporal summation, so force is graded.

open.q: Why can a whole skeletal muscle give graded contractions when a single fibre obeys the all-or-none law?
accept: number of motor units recruited varies

questions.q: A motor unit consists of:
options: A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it supplies
A single muscle fibre and several neurons
A whole muscle and its nerve
questions.explain: The motor unit is the functional unit of muscle control. All its fibres contract together when the neuron fires.

open.q: What does a motor unit consist of?
accept: motor neuron and the fibres it supplies
one motor neuron and its muscle fibres

questions.q: Which muscles have the smallest motor units (fewest fibres per motor neuron)?
questions.explain: Small motor units allow very fine control of force and movement. Large muscles used for posture and power have large motor units.

open.q: Which muscles have the smallest motor units?

questions.q: As the force demanded of a muscle increases, motor units are recruited:
questions.explain: This is Henneman's size principle. Small motor neurons are more excitable, so they fire first. They supply slow, fatigue-resistant fibres.

open.q: As the demanded force increases, in what order are motor units recruited?

questions.q: A person holds a heavy book steady with the arm outstretched. This contraction is mainly:
questions.explain: In an isometric contraction tension rises while muscle length stays the same. In an isotonic contraction the muscle shortens against a constant load.

open.q: A person holds a heavy book steady with the arm outstretched. What type of contraction is this mainly?

questions.q: Maximum active tension in skeletal muscle is developed at a sarcomere length of about:
options: 2.0–2.2 µm, where overlap of thick and thin filaments is optimal
questions.explain: At long lengths the overlap falls, so fewer cross-bridges can form, and at about 3.6 µm there is none. At very short lengths the filaments crowd and interfere with each other.

open.q: At what sarcomere length is maximum active tension developed?
open.a: About 2.0–2.2 µm, where overlap of thick and thin filaments is optimal

questions.q: Which of these is a recognised contributor to muscle fatigue in sustained strenuous exercise?
options: Accumulation of lactic acid (H⁺) and inorganic phosphate, and depletion of glycogen and ATP
An increase in pH inside the fibre
questions.explain: Fatigue is multifactorial. Metabolic changes within the fibre, together with reduced transmission at the neuromuscular junction and central factors, all contribute.

open.q: Name recognised contributors to muscle fatigue in sustained strenuous exercise.

questions.q: Muscle tone is:
options: A sustained partial contraction of a resting muscle, maintained by stretch reflex activity
questions.explain: Alternating motor units contract asynchronously, so the muscle stays firm without fatiguing. Tone is lost (flaccidity) if the motor nerve to the muscle is damaged.

open.q: What is muscle tone?

questions.q: During muscle contraction the length of the A band:
questions.explain: The A band is the length of the thick filaments, and the filaments themselves do not shorten.

open.q: During muscle contraction, what happens to the length of the A band?

questions.q: During contraction, which of these shortens or disappears?
questions.explain: Thin filaments slide into the A band, so the I band narrows and the H zone shrinks or disappears. The Z lines move closer together.

open.q: During contraction, which regions shorten or disappear?

questions.q: According to the sliding filament theory, contraction occurs because:
options: Thin filaments slide over thick filaments, pulling the Z lines together, while filament lengths stay constant
questions.explain: Cross-bridges repeatedly attach, pull and release, ratcheting the thin filaments toward the centre of the sarcomere.

open.q: According to the sliding filament theory, why does contraction occur?
accept: thin filaments slide over thick filaments

questions.q: Which is the correct order of events in excitation–contraction coupling?
options: Action potential → T tubule depolarisation → Ca²⁺ release from SR → Ca²⁺ binds troponin C → cross-bridge formation
Ca²⁺ release from SR → action potential → Ca²⁺ binds troponin C → T tubule depolarisation
Ca²⁺ binds troponin C → action potential → T tubule depolarisation → Ca²⁺ release
Cross-bridge formation → Ca²⁺ release → action potential
questions.explain: The electrical event comes first and the mechanical event follows. The delay between them is the latent period.

open.q: State the order of events in excitation–contraction coupling.
accept: action potential t tubule calcium release calcium binds troponin cross-bridge

questions.q: In skeletal muscle, calcium release from the SR is triggered by:
options: Voltage-sensing dihydropyridine receptors in the T tubule coupled directly to ryanodine receptors in the SR
Calcium entry from outside the cell through L-type channels (calcium-induced calcium release)
questions.explain: In skeletal muscle, depolarisation of the T tubule changes the conformation of the DHPR, which opens RyR1 directly. Calcium-induced calcium release is the mechanism in cardiac muscle.

open.q: What triggers calcium release from the SR in skeletal muscle?
accept: DHP receptor coupled to ryanodine receptor

questions.q: At rest, contraction is prevented because:
options: Tropomyosin covers the myosin-binding sites on actin
Troponin C is saturated with calcium
The myosin heads have no ATP
questions.explain: With low sarcoplasmic Ca²⁺, the troponin–tropomyosin complex blocks the active sites on actin.

open.q: At rest, what prevents contraction?

questions.q: Calcium binding to troponin C causes:
options: A conformational change that moves tropomyosin and exposes the active sites on actin
Release of Ca²⁺ from the SR
questions.explain: Once the active sites are uncovered, the myosin heads can bind actin and the cross-bridge cycle begins.

open.q: What does calcium binding to troponin C cause?

questions.q: Binding of a fresh ATP molecule to the myosin head causes:
options: Detachment of the head from actin
questions.explain: ATP is needed to release the cross-bridge. Hydrolysis of ATP then re-cocks the head so it can bind actin again.

open.q: What does binding of a fresh ATP molecule to the myosin head cause?

questions.q: The power stroke of the cross-bridge cycle is associated with release of:
options: Phosphate (Pi) and ADP from the myosin head
questions.explain: When the cocked head binds actin, Pi and then ADP are released and the head swivels, pulling the thin filament toward the M line.

open.q: The power stroke of the cross-bridge cycle is associated with release of what?

questions.q: Relaxation of skeletal muscle begins when calcium is:
options: Actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by the SERCA Ca²⁺-ATPase
questions.explain: As sarcoplasmic Ca²⁺ falls, it dissociates from troponin C, tropomyosin covers the active sites again, and the muscle relaxes. Relaxation is an active, ATP-dependent process.

open.q: How does relaxation of skeletal muscle begin?
open.a: Calcium is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by the SERCA Ca²⁺-ATPase

questions.q: Rigor mortis occurs after death because:
options: ATP is depleted, so myosin heads cannot detach from actin
Calcium is pumped out of the SR
questions.explain: Without ATP, the cross-bridges stay attached, and calcium leaks into the sarcoplasm. The stiffness passes only when the proteins break down.

open.q: Why does rigor mortis occur?
accept: no ATP so myosin cannot detach

questions.q: Which store provides the fastest regeneration of ATP in contracting muscle without needing oxygen?
questions.explain: Creatine phosphate donates its phosphate to ADP (the Lohmann reaction). The store lasts only a few seconds of intense effort.

open.q: Which store provides the fastest regeneration of ATP in contracting muscle without needing oxygen?

questions.q: Lactic acid forms in working muscle mainly when:
options: Oxygen supply is inadequate and glycolysis is anaerobic
questions.explain: Pyruvate is converted to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase, which regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.

open.q: When does lactic acid form in working muscle mainly?

questions.q: Recovery heat of muscle is produced:
options: After contraction, during oxidative restoration of ATP and creatine phosphate, and it needs oxygen
questions.explain: Initial heat is released during contraction and relaxation as ATP is split, and it does not need oxygen. Recovery heat is released later, as oxidative metabolism restores the energy stores.

open.q: When is recovery heat produced?

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of the energy used by a contracting muscle appears as external work?
questions.explain: Most of the remaining energy appears as heat, which is why muscles warm up during exercise and why shivering raises body temperature.

open.q: What fraction of the energy used by a contracting muscle appears as external work?

questions.q: In a skeletal muscle fibre, the action potential relative to the mechanical contraction:
options: Precedes it, with the latent period in between
Occurs at exactly the same moment
questions.explain: The fibre action potential lasts only a few milliseconds and is over before the force peaks.

open.q: Relative to the mechanical contraction, when does the action potential occur in a skeletal muscle fibre?
open.a: It precedes it, with the latent period in between

questions.q: Which structural feature distinguishes cardiac muscle fibers from both skeletal and smooth muscle fibers?
options: Multinucleated fibres with peripheral nuclei and no intercalated discs
Branched, striated cells with central nuclei and intercalated discs; T-tubules form diads at Z-lines
Spindle-shaped cells without sarcomeres or troponin
Striated fibres with triads at every Z-line and multiple peripheral nuclei
questions.explain: Cardiac myocytes are branched, mononucleated (or binucleated) striated cells joined end-to-end by intercalated discs (fascia adherens, desmosomes, and connexin-43 gap junctions), with wide T-tubules forming diads at the Z-lines.

open.q: State three ultrastructural features that distinguish cardiac muscle from skeletal muscle.
accept: Branched cells with central nuclei, intercalated discs (desmosomes and gap junctions), and diads (one T-tubule + one SR cisterna) located at the Z-lines
Intercalated discs, central nuclei, branched fibers, and Z-line diads

questions.q: What is the role of the connective tissue sheaths—epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium—in whole skeletal muscle?
options: They synthesize myosin and actin during each contraction
They transmit force to tendons and provide routes for blood vessels and nerves
They generate independent action potentials in the absence of motor neurons
They store most intracellular calcium outside the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explain: Endomysium surrounds individual myofibers, perimysium bundles fascicles, and epimysium invests the entire muscle belly, merging into tendons and providing passive resistance against overstretching.

open.q: Name the three connective tissue layers of skeletal muscle from outermost to innermost and state their mechanical function.
accept: Epimysium (around whole muscle), perimysium (around fascicles), and endomysium (around individual muscle fibers); they transmit contractile force to tendons and provide parallel passive elasticity
Epimysium, perimysium, endomysium; force transmission and parallel elasticity

questions.q: Which protein extends along the entire length of the thin actin filament in striated muscle and acts as a 'molecular ruler' specifying thin-filament length?
questions.explain: Nebulin is an inelastic giant protein running alongside F-actin from the Z-disc to regulate thin-filament assembly and length, whereas titin spans from Z-disc to M-line along thick myosin filaments.

open.q: Name the sarcomeric protein that runs along thin actin filaments to regulate their length.

questions.q: What are the enzymatic and structural components of a single myosin II molecule?
options: Two heavy chains form the tail and two ATPase/actin-binding heads; four light chains bind the heads
A single globular chain contains four calcium-binding sites and no ATPase activity
Seven actin monomers form a double helix with two tropomyosin strands
A transmembrane protein forms a sodium-selective pore in the sarcolemma
questions.explain: Trypsin and papain cleavage divide myosin II into light meromyosin (tail forming the thick filament backbone) and heavy meromyosin (S2 hinge + two S1 globular heads harboring actin-binding and ATPase catalytic sites). Key detail: Two heavy chains form a coiled-coil tail and two actin-binding ATPase heads; four light chains associate with the heads.

open.q: State the two functional binding sites located on each globular S1 head of a myosin II heavy chain.
accept: An actin-binding site and an ATP-binding / ATPase catalytic site
Actin-binding site and myosin ATPase site

questions.q: How does calcium mobilization during excitation-contraction coupling differ fundamentally between skeletal muscle and cardiac muscle?
options: Skeletal muscle requires extracellular calcium entry to trigger SR release; cardiac muscle uses direct DHP-RyR coupling
Skeletal: mechanical DHP–RyR1 coupling; cardiac: Ca2+ entry via Cav1.2 triggers RyR2-mediated CICR
Neither muscle type uses sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium stores
questions.explain: Because cardiac muscle depends on extracellular Ca2+ entry during the action potential plateau to trigger CICR via RyR2, cardiac contractility is directly sensitive to extracellular [Ca2+] and L-type Ca2+ channel blockers (verapamil/diltiazem), unlike skeletal muscle. Key detail: Skeletal muscle uses mechanical Cav1.1-RyR1 coupling; cardiac muscle uses calcium entry through Cav1.2 to trigger CICR via RyR2.

open.q: Explain why removing extracellular Ca2+ immediately abolishes cardiac muscle contraction while skeletal muscle continues to contract for many twitches.
accept: Cardiac muscle requires extracellular Ca2+ influx through L-type channels to trigger calcium-induced calcium release (CICR) from RyR2, whereas skeletal muscle uses direct mechanical coupling between DHP sensors and RyR1
Cardiac CICR depends on transmembrane Ca2+ entry; skeletal muscle uses mechanical DHP-RyR1 coupling

questions.q: How does beta-adrenergic stimulation (norepinephrine/epinephrine acting on beta-1 receptors) enhance both the force (inotropy) and relaxation speed (lusitropy) of cardiac muscle?
options: β₁–Gs–cAMP–PKA signalling increases Ca²⁺ entry and relieves phospholamban inhibition of SERCA2a
β₁–Gi signalling closes L-type Ca²⁺ channels and inhibits SERCA2a
β₁ stimulation blocks ryanodine receptors and prevents calcium release from the SR
β₁ stimulation degrades troponin C and slows cross-bridge cycling
questions.explain: Unphosphorylated phospholamban inhibits cardiac SERCA2a; PKA phosphorylation of phospholamban accelerates SR Ca2+ reuptake (faster relaxation/lusitropy) while loading larger SR Ca2+ stores for subsequent beats (positive inotropy).

open.q: What is the role of phospholamban in cardiac muscle, and how does its phosphorylation by protein kinase A affect cardiac relaxation?
accept: Unphosphorylated phospholamban inhibits SERCA2a; PKA phosphorylation relieves this inhibition, accelerating SR Ca2+ reuptake and speeding myocardial relaxation (positive lusitropy)
Phospholamban regulates SERCA2a; phosphorylation speeds Ca2+ sequestration into the SR

questions.q: During the cross-bridge cycle, which exact biochemical step triggers the mechanical 'power stroke' (rotation of the myosin lever arm pulling actin toward the M-line)?
options: Binding of unhydrolyzed ATP to the myosin head
Hydrolysis of ATP into ADP and Pi prior to actin attachment
Pi release from actin-bound myosin-ADP-Pi triggers the power stroke
Binding of Ca2+ directly to the myosin light chain in skeletal muscle
questions.explain: ATP hydrolysis cocks the myosin head before strong actin binding; once Ca2+ uncovers actin sites and myosin binds weakly, release of Pi triggers the conformational power stroke, followed by ADP release leaving myosin tightly bound until a new ATP binds. Key detail: Release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) from the myosin-ADP-Pi complex upon tight binding to actin, followed by ADP release.

open.q: Place these four steps of the skeletal muscle cross-bridge cycle in correct sequential order: (A) Power stroke upon Pi release, (B) ATP binding and myosin detachment from actin, (C) Cross-bridge binding to actin, (D) ATP hydrolysis cocking the myosin head.
accept: ATP binding/detachment, ATP hydrolysis/cocking, actin binding, Pi release/power stroke

questions.q: In a whole skeletal muscle length-tension curve, how is 'active tension' experimentally determined at any given muscle length?
options: Active tension equals passive tension measured before stimulation
Active tension equals total stimulated tension minus passive tension at the same muscle length
Active tension equals maximal shortening velocity divided by the applied load
Active tension equals resting tension multiplied by the number of motor units
questions.explain: As a muscle is stretched beyond its resting equilibrium length, passive tension (from titin and extracellular collagen) rises exponentially; subtracting passive tension from total stimulated tension isolates true cross-bridge active tension.

open.q: How is active tension calculated from total tension and passive tension on a whole skeletal muscle length-tension diagram?
accept: Active tension = Total tension minus Passive tension
Subtracting passive resting tension from total stimulated tension at each muscle length

questions.q: Why does cardiac muscle normally operate on the ascending limb of its length-tension curve (Frank-Starling mechanism), and why is it far stiffer passively than skeletal muscle?
options: Cardiac muscle lacks titin and collagen
Stiff titin/collagen and short resting sarcomeres limit stretch while allowing preload recruitment
Cardiac muscle has no sarcoplasmic reticulum
Cardiac muscle generates maximal force at zero preload
questions.explain: High passive stiffness prevents cardiac sarcomeres from slipping onto the descending limb during ventricular filling, while stretch enhances troponin C Ca2+ affinity and optimal filament geometry (length-dependent activation). Key detail: Short resting sarcomeres, stiff titin and collagen permit preload recruitment while limiting overstretch.

open.q: Explain the sarcomeric basis of the Frank-Starling law of the heart (length-dependent activation).
accept: Increased end-diastolic ventricular volume stretches myocardial sarcomeres toward optimal length (~2.2 um), improving thick-thin filament overlap and increasing troponin C sensitivity to Ca2+
Greater sarcomere stretch improves cross-bridge overlap and myofilament Ca2+ sensitivity

questions.q: What is the 'Fenn effect' in contracting skeletal muscle?
options: Work-performing muscle releases more total energy than isometric muscle
Skeletal muscle stops consuming oxygen during running
Resting muscle produces more heat than maximally contracting muscle
External load has no effect on muscle ATP hydrolysis rate
questions.explain: Wallace Fenn demonstrated that shortening and performing work accelerates cross-bridge cycling and myosin ATPase turnover, increasing total energy liberation above isometric maintenance heat. Key detail: A muscle performing external mechanical work liberates MORE total energy (heat + mechanical work) than a muscle contracting isometrically against an immovable load.

open.q: State the Fenn effect in skeletal muscle energetics.
accept: Total energy liberated (heat plus work) by a contracting muscle increases proportionally to the amount of external mechanical work performed compared to an isometric contraction
Work-performing isotonic contractions liberate more total energy/ATP than isometric contractions

questions.q: In skeletal muscle mechanics, at what fraction of maximal isometric force (Po) and maximal shortening velocity (Vmax) is mechanical power output (Power = Force x Velocity) maximal?
options: At zero load (Vmax) where force is zero
At maximal isometric load (Po) where velocity is zero
Peak power occurs at intermediate load and velocity, about 0.3 Po and 0.3 Vmax
questions.explain: Because Power = Force * Velocity, power is zero at both extremes (zero load and isometric load) and peaks at approximately 30% of maximal isometric force and 30% of Vmax (which is why bicycle gears keep pedaling near optimal velocity). Key detail: At intermediate load and velocity—specifically around one-third of Po (~0.3 Po) and one-third of Vmax (~0.3 Vmax).

open.q: Why is mechanical power output zero at both Vmax and Po, and approximately where along the force-velocity curve does peak power occur?
accept: Power = Force x Velocity (zero when either F=0 or V=0); peak power occurs around one-third (~30%) of maximal isometric force and Vmax
Peak power occurs at intermediate load (~0.3 Po) and intermediate velocity (~0.3 Vmax)

questions.sub: Muscle Fiber Types and Exercise Adaptation
questions.q: How do Type IIa (fast oxidative-glycolytic) skeletal muscle fibers compare metabolically and functionally with Type I and Type IIx/IIb fibers?
options: Type IIa fibres are fast, oxidative-glycolytic and moderately fatigue-resistant
Type IIa fibers have the slowest myosin ATPase of all fiber types
Type IIa fibers lack mitochondria and glycogen completely
Type IIa fibers are found exclusively in smooth muscle
questions.explain: Type IIa fibers represent an adaptable intermediate fast-twitch phenotype: endurance training shifts Type IIx fibers toward Type IIa oxidative capacity, whereas resistance training induces myofibrillar hypertrophy across Type II fibers. Key detail: Type IIa fibers combine fast myosin heavy-chain ATPase speed with moderate-to-high mitochondrial oxidative capacity and myoglobin, giving high force with intermediate fatigue resistance.

open.q: Compare the three human skeletal muscle fiber types (Type I, Type IIa, Type IIx) in terms of contraction speed and fatigue resistance.
accept: Type I: slow contraction, high fatigue resistance; Type IIa: fast contraction, intermediate/high fatigue resistance; Type IIx: fastest contraction, low fatigue resistance (fatigues rapidly)
Type I slow/fatigue-resistant, Type IIa fast oxidative/moderately fatigue-resistant, Type IIx fast glycolytic/rapidly fatiguing

questions.sub: Muscle Fiber Types and Exercise Adaptation
questions.q: What is the primary cellular difference between skeletal muscle 'hypertrophy' induced by heavy resistance training and 'hyperplasia'?
options: Hypertrophy enlarges existing fibres; hyperplasia increases fibre number and is limited in adult human muscle
Hypertrophy increases fibre number; hyperplasia enlarges each existing fibre
Both processes increase muscle size only by retaining intracellular water
Hyperplasia is the main response to resistance training in adult skeletal muscle
questions.explain: Post-mitotic skeletal myofibers enlarge primarily by mTORC1-driven myofibrillar protein synthesis and fusion of quiescent Pax7+ satellite cells donating new myonuclei to maintain the myonuclear domain.

open.q: Define muscle hypertrophy and state the role of satellite cells in skeletal muscle growth and repair.
accept: Hypertrophy is enlargement of existing muscle fibers via increased parallel myofibrils/sarcomeres; Pax7+ satellite cells proliferate and fuse with myofibers to donate new nuclei and regenerate damaged fibers
Increase in individual myofiber cross-sectional area; satellite cells act as myogenic stem cells for repair and myonuclear addition

questions.sub: Muscle Fiber Types and Exercise Adaptation
questions.q: What occurs during 'disuse atrophy' and 'denervation atrophy' of skeletal muscle?
options: Disuse increases protein breakdown; denervation adds fibrillations and extrajunctional ACh receptors
Denervated muscle doubles in mass and develops stronger tetanic force
Disuse atrophy increases mitochondrial density tenfold
Denervation removes all acetylcholine receptors from the sarcolemma
questions.explain: Without motor nerve trophic input and mechanical load, FoxO transcription factors upregulate muscle-specific E3 ubiquitin ligases; denervated fibers also express fetal-type nicotinic receptors across the entire sarcolemma ('denervation supersensitivity') and spontaneous single-fiber fibrillations. Key detail: Reduced loading increases muscle protein breakdown; denervation also causes spontaneous activity and extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors.

open.q: State two electrophysiological or receptor changes that develop in skeletal muscle fibers subsequent to lower motor neuron denervation.
accept: Spontaneous single-fiber fibrillation potentials on EMG and spread of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors across the extrajunctional sarcolemma (denervation supersensitivity)
Fibrillations and extrajunctional ACh receptor upregulation

questions.q: What does a clinical needle electromyogram (EMG) record, and how does the motor unit action potential (MUAP) pattern differ between a primary myopathy and chronic neurogenic denervation/reinnervation?
options: Myopathy: small, short MUAPs; chronic neurogenic disease: large, long MUAPs
EMG directly measures serum creatine kinase
Myopathy produces giant long-duration MUAPs; neuropathy produces tiny short MUAPs
Normal relaxed skeletal muscle shows continuous high-voltage fibrillation potentials
questions.explain: In myopathies, loss of individual myofibers within motor units shrinks MUAP amplitude/duration so more units must be recruited early; in chronic neuropathies, surviving motor axons sprout to reinnervate orphaned fibers, creating giant MUAPs with reduced recruitment. Key detail: EMG records muscle electrical activity; myopathy gives small, short MUAPs, while chronic neurogenic disease gives large, long MUAPs.

open.q: Contrast needle EMG motor unit action potential (MUAP) amplitude, duration, and recruitment in a primary myopathy versus chronic neurogenic denervation.
accept: Myopathy: small-amplitude, short-duration polyphasic MUAPs with early/full recruitment; Chronic neuropathy: large-amplitude, long-duration MUAPs with reduced recruitment
Small/short MUAPs with early recruitment (myopathy) vs giant/long MUAPs with reduced recruitment (neuropathy)

questions.q: Which four pathways clear cytosolic Ca2+ to allow smooth muscle relaxation once excitatory stimulation ends?
options: Only diffusion of calcium through nuclear pores
SERCA, PMCA, NCX and mitochondria lower Ca2+; MLCP dephosphorylates myosin
Opening L-type calcium channels and activating MLCK
Hydrolysis of actin by calpain proteases
questions.explain: Unlike skeletal muscle (where SERCA alone handles nearly all Ca2+ cycling), smooth muscle relies heavily on both SR SERCA and sarcolemmal Ca2+ extrusion (PMCA and NCX) plus MLCP activation to terminate contraction. Key detail: SERCA, PMCA, NCX and mitochondrial uptake lower cytosolic calcium; MLCP dephosphorylates myosin.

open.q: Name three Ca2+ transport mechanisms that lower cytosolic Ca2+ to initiate smooth muscle relaxation.
accept: SERCA (SR Ca2+-ATPase), plasma membrane Ca2+-ATPase (PMCA), and Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX)
SR Ca2+ pump, sarcolemmal Ca2+ pump, and Na+/Ca2+ exchange

questions.q: What is the 'myogenic response' (Bayliss effect) in arteriolar vascular smooth muscle?
options: Reflex vasodilation caused by parasympathetic vagal stimulation
Pressure stretch depolarises arteriolar muscle, increasing Ca2+ entry and constriction
Release of acetylcholine from vascular endothelial cells
Skeletal muscle shivering in cold weather
questions.explain: Independent of extrinsic nerves or endothelium, elevated arterial pressure stretches arteriolar smooth muscle, opening mechanosensitive channels (TRPC6/TRPM4/ENaC) and Cav1.2 channels to maintain constant renal, cerebral, and coronary blood flow. Key detail: Raised pressure stretches arteriolar smooth muscle, causing depolarisation, calcium entry and vasoconstriction.

open.q: Explain the Bayliss myogenic response in vascular smooth muscle and its physiological purpose.
accept: Increased intraluminal pressure stretches arteriolar smooth muscle, causing depolarization, Ca2+ influx, and vasoconstriction to maintain constant organ blood flow (autoregulation)
Stretch-induced intrinsic arteriolar vasoconstriction mediating blood flow autoregulation

questions.q: Compare the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) abundance and T-tubule presence across skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle.
options: Skeletal: abundant SR and T-tubules; cardiac: moderate SR and T-tubules; smooth: sparse SR with caveolae.
Smooth muscle has the most extensive T-tubule system
Cardiac ventricular myocytes have no T-tubules
questions.explain: Because skeletal fibers are large (up to 100 um diameter) and contract rapidly without extracellular Ca2+, they require dense SR stores and rapid T-tubule conduction; small spindle-shaped smooth muscle cells (2-10 um) rely largely on extracellular Ca2+ entry. Key detail: Skeletal: extensive SR and T-tubules; cardiac: moderate SR and T-tubules; smooth: sparse SR and caveolae instead of T-tubules.

open.q: Compare T-tubule presence and sarcoplasmic reticulum development among skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle.
accept: Skeletal: extensive SR, narrow T-tubules at A-I junctions; Cardiac: moderate SR, wide T-tubules at Z-lines; Smooth: sparse peripheral SR, no T-tubules (caveolae instead)
Skeletal has abundant SR and A-I T-tubules; cardiac has moderate SR and Z-line T-tubules; smooth has scant SR and no T-tubules

questions.q: Why does 'delayed-onset muscle soreness' (DOMS) peak 24 to 72 hours after unaccustomed eccentric exercise (such as downhill running or lowering heavy weights)?
options: DOMS results from lactic acid remaining trapped in muscle for several days
Eccentric contractions cause sarcomere/Z-disc microdamage and delayed inflammation
DOMS is caused by complete interruption of arterial supply during exercise
DOMS results from conversion of muscle fibres into fibrous connective tissue
questions.explain: Blood and muscle lactate return to baseline within 1 hour of exercise; DOMS reflects ultrastructural sarcomere microdamage and sterile inflammatory repair triggered by high-force eccentric strain. Key detail: Eccentric loading causes sarcomere and Z-disc microdamage, followed by local inflammation and nociceptor sensitization.

open.q: Why are eccentric contractions more likely to cause delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) than concentric contractions, and why is lactic acid NOT the cause?
accept: Eccentric lengthening places higher mechanical force per active cross-bridge, causing Z-disc/sarcolemmal microdamage and delayed inflammation; lactate is cleared within an hour of exercise
Mechanical sarcomere microtrauma and inflammation from high eccentric tension, whereas lactate clears rapidly post-exercise

questions.q: How do 'preload' and 'afterload' affect skeletal muscle contraction mechanics in an isolated muscle lever experiment?
options: Preload sets initial muscle length; afterload is the external load that must be overcome before shortening begins
Preload is the load lifted during shortening; afterload is the resting membrane potential
Preload determines only shortening velocity; afterload determines resting sarcomere length
Preload and afterload both refer to the passive tension measured before stimulation
questions.explain: During an afterloaded isotonic twitch, the muscle first contracts isometrically until active tension equals afterload, then shortens isotonically; higher afterload prolongs the isometric phase and slows shortening velocity.

open.q: Distinguish preload from afterload in skeletal or cardiac muscle mechanics.
accept: Preload is the passive load stretching the muscle prior to contraction (determining resting sarcomere length); afterload is the load against which the muscle contracts after stimulation begins
Preload stretches resting muscle before contraction; afterload opposes shortening during contraction

questions.q: A 22-year-old man presents with progressive inability to relax his grip after shaking hands (grip myotonia), frontal balding, cataracts, cardiac conduction block, and distal muscle weakness. Genetic testing shows an expanded CTG trinucleotide repeat in the DMPK gene (myotonic dystrophy type 1). What is the molecular pathogenesis of myotonic dystrophy type 1?
options: CUG-repeat RNA sequesters MBNL1, disrupting ClC-1 splicing and reducing chloride conductance.
Complete absence of dystrophin protein at the Z-disc
Autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type calcium channels
questions.explain: Normally, high resting Cl- conductance (~70-80% of resting sarcolemmal conductance) stabilizes skeletal muscle membrane potential against K+ buildup inside narrow T-tubules during repetitive firing; loss of ClC-1 channels causes T-tubular K+ depolarization to trigger after-discharges (myotonia). Key detail: Expanded CUG-repeat RNA sequesters MBNL1, disrupting ClC-1 splicing and reducing muscle chloride conductance.

open.q: Explain why skeletal muscle normally has an unusually high resting Cl- permeability (~70-80% of resting conductance) and what happens when ClC-1 channels are lost (myotonia congenita / myotonic dystrophy).
accept: High resting Cl- conductance stabilizes membrane potential against K+ accumulation inside T-tubules during repetitive activity; loss of Cl- channels allows T-tubular K+ depolarization to trigger repetitive firing and delayed relaxation (myotonia)
Stabilizes resting potential against T-tubular K+ buildup; deficiency causes hyperexcitability and myotonia

questions.q: A 17-year-old male athlete develops severe painful muscle cramps, dark tea-colored urine (myoglobinuria), and a 'second-wind' phenomenon (marked improvement in exercise tolerance after ~10 minutes of moderate exertion) during sprint workouts. Forearm ischemic exercise testing shows no rise in venous lactate. Which enzyme deficiency causes McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V)?
options: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency prevents muscle glycogen use during exercise.
questions.explain: Without myophosphorylase, skeletal muscle cannot mobilize endogenous glycogen for rapid anaerobic glycolysis at exercise onset, causing cramps and rhabdomyolysis until exercise-induced vasodilation supplies exogenous blood glucose and fatty acids. Key detail: Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency limits glycogen use during exercise, causing cramps and a second-wind phenomenon.

open.q: Identify the deficient enzyme in McArdle disease and explain the physiological basis of its characteristic 'second-wind' phenomenon.
accept: Skeletal muscle glycogen phosphorylase (myophosphorylase); after ~10 minutes, increased muscle blood flow delivers blood-borne glucose and free fatty acids to bypass the block in endogenous glycogen breakdown
Muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency; resolved transiently when hyperemia supplies exogenous glucose and fatty acids

questions.q: A 38-year-old man is trapped under collapsed concrete for 8 hours following an earthquake. Shortly after extrication, he develops dark brown urine, oliguric acute kidney injury, serum creatine kinase of 85,000 U/L, and peaked T waves with serum K+ of 7.4 mEq/L. What is the pathophysiological cascade of traumatic rhabdomyolysis?
options: ATP depletion causes Ca²⁺ overload and myocyte rupture, releasing K⁺ and myoglobin.
Excess dystrophin synthesis damages renal tubules
Hyperpolarisation of muscle membranes to −150 mV
questions.explain: Skeletal muscle holds the body's largest intracellular K+ and myoglobin stores; sarcolemmal rupture releases K+ (causing fatal arrhythmias) and myoglobin (causing renal tubular obstruction, heme-induced free radical injury, and renal vasoconstriction). Key detail: ATP depletion impairs ion pumps, causing calcium overload, muscle breakdown and release of potassium and myoglobin.

open.q: Explain why extensive skeletal muscle crush injury (rhabdomyolysis) causes both life-threatening hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury.
accept: Ruptured myocytes release abundant intracellular K+ into plasma (hyperkalemia) and large amounts of myoglobin, which precipitates in renal tubules and causes heme-mediated tubular toxicity
Leakage of intracellular K+ and nephrotoxic myoglobin from necrotic muscle fibers

questions.q: A 52-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus treated with high-dose oral prednisone for 6 months develops insidious symmetric proximal hip and shoulder weakness (difficulty climbing stairs and combing hair) with normal serum creatine kinase and normal nerve conduction studies. Which mechanism explains steroid myopathy?
options: Glucocorticoids increase protein breakdown and suppress synthesis, preferentially atrophying type II fibres.
Autoantibodies destroy postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
A gain-of-function mutation in RyR1 causes sustained calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Demyelination of dorsal root ganglia prevents sensory conduction to proximal muscles
questions.explain: Exogenous or endogenous glucocorticoids (Cushing syndrome) stimulate myofibrillar protein breakdown and inhibit amino acid uptake, preferentially shrinking fast-twitch Type II fibers without inflammatory necrosis (so serum CK remains normal). Key detail: Glucocorticoids increase ubiquitin–proteasome protein breakdown and suppress IGF-1/mTOR synthesis, preferentially atrophying fast fibres.

open.q: Which skeletal muscle fiber type is preferentially atrophied in glucocorticoid-induced (steroid) myopathy, and why is serum creatine kinase typically normal?
accept: Type II (fast glycolytic) fibers; serum CK is normal because muscle weakness results from non-inflammatory protein catabolism/atrophy rather than sarcolemmal necrosis
Type II fast fibers; non-necrotic protein breakdown preserves sarcolemmal integrity

questions.q: A 46-year-old woman presents with progressive painless proximal muscle weakness, heliotrope violaceous rash around the eyelids, Gottron papules over the knuckles, and elevated serum creatine kinase (4,200 U/L). Muscle biopsy shows perifascicular atrophy and perivascular CD4+ T-cell/B-cell infiltrates with complement membrane attack complex deposition in endomysial capillaries. What is the diagnosis?
options: Dermatomyositis: complement-mediated capillary injury causes perifascicular atrophy.
questions.explain: Dermatomyositis is an idiopathic inflammatory myopathy characterized by humoral complement-mediated destruction of endomysial capillaries causing perifascicular atrophy and classic cutaneous findings, whereas polymyositis involves direct CD8+ T-cell invasion of healthy MHC-I-expressing myofibers. Key detail: Dermatomyositis (complement-mediated microangiopathy leading to perifascicular myofiber ischemia and necrosis).

open.q: Contrast the primary immunopathological mechanisms of dermatomyositis versus polymyositis on muscle biopsy.
accept: Dermatomyositis: humoral complement-mediated microangiopathy of endomysial capillaries causing perifascicular atrophy; Polymyositis: direct CD8+ cytotoxic T-cell invasion of endomysial myofibers
Perivascular humoral capillary attack with perifascicular atrophy (dermatomyositis) vs endomysial CD8+ T-cell myofiber invasion (polymyositis)

questions.q: A patient develops fatigable ptosis and diplopia that worsen toward evening. Autoantibodies impair the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Which physiological change explains the weakness?
options: Smaller end-plate potentials are less likely to reach the threshold for a muscle action potential.
Increased acetylcholine release from motor nerve terminals
Prolonged opening of voltage-gated sodium channels in the muscle membrane
Increased calcium sensitivity of the contractile proteins
questions.explain: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce functional postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors. The end-plate potential is smaller, so it may fail to reach threshold and trigger a muscle action potential, particularly with repeated activity.

open.q: Why does loss of postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors cause fatigable weakness in myasthenia gravis?
accept: reduced end plate potential may fail to reach threshold
fewer ACh receptors reduce end plate potential amplitude

questions.q: After several weeks of endurance training, a healthy student can sustain a higher workload before becoming markedly breathless. Which adaptation most directly increases the capacity of skeletal muscle to use oxygen during prolonged exercise?
options: Increased mitochondrial density and oxidative enzyme activity
Reduced capillary supply to active muscle
A shift of all muscle fibres to fast glycolytic type IIx fibres
questions.explain: Endurance training increases mitochondrial density, oxidative enzyme activity and capillary supply in trained muscle. These adaptations improve aerobic ATP production and fatigue resistance during prolonged exercise.

questions.q: During an incremental exercise test, blood lactate begins to rise disproportionately as workload increases. Which explanation best accounts for this lactate threshold?
options: Lactate production and appearance in blood begin to exceed its removal and oxidation
Skeletal muscle stops using glucose completely
Oxygen delivery to every muscle fibre falls to zero
The liver stops taking up lactate at all exercise intensities
questions.explain: Lactate threshold reflects the exercise intensity at which lactate appearance in blood rises faster than its clearance and oxidation. It is not simply the point at which oxygen is absent; lactate is produced and used even during aerobic exercise.
